metaDescription: Six heavy-duty kitchen shears compared on blade steel, thickness, hardness and handle build, from MAD SHARK and HOSHANHO to SHAN ZU and Gidli.
introParagraphs: Heavy duty is a phrase every listing uses, which makes it nearly meaningless until you look at the numbers behind it. A genuinely heavy-duty kitchen shear has a blade thick enough to resist flexing, steel hard enough to hold an edge, a pivot that does not loosen and handles that stay comfortable when you lean into a cut. Many pairs that carry the label are simply standard shears with a bolder name.

We evaluated six distinct pairs that make a credible case for heavy use: the MAD SHARK poultry shears at 3.5mm, the HOSHANHO with a Pakkawood handle and 57 HRC steel, the SHAN ZU titanium-plated pair, the Gidli two-piece set, the DRAGON RIOT German stainless shears and the Astercook three-pack. The comparison draws on product specs and buyer feedback on each listing, and it concentrates on thickness, hardness, handle construction and how each pair comes clean.

The right pair depends on how hard you really push it. Cutting chicken backbones is a different job from trimming herbs, and a pair built for one will often be clumsy at the other. Before you buy, write down the single toughest thing you cut each month, because that task, not the average one, is what a heavy-duty shear should be chosen for. A pair that handles that job comfortably will manage everything else without complaint.

products.name: MAD SHARK Heavy Duty Poultry Shears
products.description:
The MAD SHARK is the pair to choose if heavy duty means bones. Precision-tempered 3.5mm blades in rust-proof molybdenum-vanadium steel stay rigid on joints and backbones, and spring-loaded handles reopen the blades after every squeeze.

A thumb-activated safety lock holds the shears closed, and the listing describes it as quick to operate with one hand. The maker also mentions a built-in nut cracker, which makes it a useful tool for holiday cooking. The tradeoff is size and weight, since this is a dedicated poultry shear and not a drawer all-rounder.

In use it will outperform the lighter Gidli on bone work, though it lacks the Gidli seafood scissor. Against the HOSHANHO at 57 HRC it offers a thicker stated blade while the HOSHANHO offers a stated hardness. It is the most capable pair in the lineup for raw cutting power.
products.bestFor: Cooks who regularly cut through bones and joints.
cons: Spring and lock add moving parts

products.name: HOSHANHO Heavy Duty Kitchen Scissors
products.description:
The HOSHANHO uses 5Cr15MoV stainless steel that is heat-treated to 57 HRC, a hardness on the high side for kitchen shears. The handle is Pakkawood with full-tang construction, which the maker says adds balance and stability.

A built-in lock-safe mechanism keeps the blades closed during storage. The listing says it is easy to clean, though it does not describe a take-apart design in the excerpt we reviewed. The wood-composite handle brings a premium feel that plastic-handled pairs do not match.

The tradeoff is that hard steel can chip if twisted against bone, and a wooden handle deserves hand washing rather than a dishwasher. Compared with the SHAN ZU at 57 HRC it matches the hardness but adds a lock and a premium handle. It is the best pick for buyers who want a tool that feels special.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want a hard steel blade and a premium handle.
cons: Hard steel can chip if twisted on bone

products.name: SHAN ZU 8.4 Inch Titanium Kitchen Scissors
products.description:
The SHAN ZU is a full-size 8.4 inch shear in 5Cr15MoV steel at 57 HRC, with a titanium coating on the blades. The maker says the detachable design eliminates hidden corners for a deeper, more hygienic clean.

That detachable feature is the key difference from the HOSHANHO, which does not describe a take-apart pivot. The listing also calls the shears dishwasher safe, so it works for cooks who wash everything in the machine. A harder steel holds an edge longer but is less forgiving of twisting against bone.

It competes with the HOSHANHO on hardness and with the Gidli on cleaning. Against the Gidli it is a single heavy shear rather than a two-piece set. It is a strong choice if you want the strongest edge with the easiest cleaning in a single tool.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want hard steel and detachable cleaning in one tool.
pros: 57 HRC steel for long edge life
cons: Not built for heavy bone work

products.name: Gidli Kitchen Shears and Seafood Scissors Set
products.description:
The Gidli set provides an 8 inch all-purpose shear with a protective sheath and a 7 inch seafood scissor, both in 3Cr13 stainless steel. TPR and PP handles suit left and right hands, and the main shears weigh 4.8 oz.

The set is aimed at cooks who want two purpose-built tools rather than one heavy shear. The lifetime replacement guarantee on the listing is a nice reassurance. The steel is a common mid-range grade that is easy to resharpen but will not match 57 HRC for edge life.

Compared with the MAD SHARK it is lighter and more versatile, but it is not meant for heavy bone work. Against the Astercook three-pack it gives two different tools rather than three similar ones. It is a practical choice for everyday heavy-ish jobs.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want a light shear plus a seafood scissor.
pros: Lifetime replacement guarantee on the listing
cons: Not meant for heavy bone cutting

products.name: DRAGON RIOT Heavy Duty Poultry Shears Set
products.description:
The DRAGON RIOT set uses German stainless steel with micro-serrated edges for non-slip cutting. The maker says the shears are bigger and stronger than regular kitchen shears, and a matching seafood scissor is included.

Soft secure grips are listed on both tools, and the shears are described as dishwasher safe. The listing does not publish thickness or hardness, so it is harder to compare directly with the MAD SHARK or HOSHANHO. It does offer a practical combination for cooks who handle poultry and shellfish.

In ownership terms it is a simple, ready-to-use set. Compared with the Gidli it adds German steel and serrations, and against the Astercook it is a two-piece set with a specialised tool. It suits buyers who want a set rather than a single heavy shear.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want a poultry shear plus seafood scissors in one set.
cons: Less detail than the premium pairs

products.name: Astercook 3-Pack Heavy Duty Kitchen Shears
products.description:
The Astercook set gives you three pairs of heavy duty shears with different handle colors. The maker suggests dedicating one pair to meat and seafood, another to vegetables and herbs and a third to general use.

That colour system helps with food hygiene, because each task has its own tool. The shears are described as having a solid, sturdy feel with lasting sharpness, but the listing does not publish blade thickness or steel grade. That means it is better thought of as a practical household set than as a bone-cutting specialist.

Compared with the MAD SHARK it has less raw power, and against the Gidli it offers more pairs but fewer special tools. It suits large households that want multiple shears ready to go. Check the listing before buying if you need specifics on weight or length.
products.bestFor: Large households that want a pair for each task.
cons: No steel grade or thickness listed

buyingCriteria.explanation: Thickness is the clearest sign of a heavy-duty blade, because a thicker blade resists flexing under load. The MAD SHARK lists 3.5mm tempered blades, which sit at the top of this lineup. The HOSHANHO, SHAN ZU, Gidli, DRAGON RIOT and Astercook do not publish a thickness figure. If you plan to cut bones, favour the stated 3.5mm and treat unlisted thickness as unknown. A thick blade also adds weight, so consider how long you will hold the shears. If the listing is silent on thickness, as it is for the Astercook and DRAGON RIOT, assume a standard kitchen blade and keep bone work for the MAD SHARK. Rocking a pair gently in your hand in a shop, if you can, tells you a lot about stiffness.

Hardness around 53 to 57 HRC balances edge retention with chip resistance. The HOSHANHO and SHAN ZU both list 5Cr15MoV at 57 HRC, while the Gidli uses 3Cr13, which is softer but easier to resharpen. Harder steel holds an edge longer but can chip if twisted against bone. Cut straight along the line of the bone to protect the edge. A mid-range steel that you can resharpen at home is often more practical than a very hard steel you hesitate to touch up. Match the steel to how much maintenance you are willing to do.

A heavy-duty shear needs a handle that will not loosen or crack. The HOSHANHO uses a Pakkawood full-tang handle, the Gidli uses TPR and PP, and the MAD SHARK offers spring-loaded handles. Wood-composite handles need hand washing, while plastic handles tolerate the dishwasher. Check how the handle is attached to the blade, since a full tang is generally sturdier. Check how the handle meets the blade, because a loose rivet or a cracked grip is the usual first failure on a heavy shear. A full-tang design like the HOSHANHO spreads the load along the handle.

The pivot takes the load of every cut and also hides residue. The SHAN ZU is detachable for deep cleaning, while others have fixed pivots. A fixed pivot is often stiffer, but it relies on thorough washing. Follow USDA guidance when the shears touch raw poultry. If you wash by hand, a fixed pivot is fine as long as you flush it with hot water and dry it open. Detachable pairs make that routine easier but add a step at reassembly.

Heavy shears are more dangerous to store loose. The MAD SHARK and HOSHANHO list locks, and the Gidli includes a protective sheath. A lock keeps the blades closed and the edge protected. Pick the storage style that fits your drawer. A lock matters most if the shears live in a drawer with other tools. A sheath such as the Gidli's does the same job for a pair without a lock.

A set can suit a household better than one big tool. The Gidli and DRAGON RIOT add seafood scissors, and the Astercook includes three pairs. A single heavy shear such as the MAD SHARK focuses all the quality in one tool. Decide whether you want versatility or maximum capability. If you share a kitchen, colour coding like the Astercook adds a visible rule that is easy for everyone to follow.

faq.q: What makes kitchen shears heavy duty?
faq.a: A heavy-duty shear has a thicker blade, harder steel and a sturdy pivot and handle. The MAD SHARK lists 3.5mm blades, and the HOSHANHO and SHAN ZU list 57 HRC. The label alone proves nothing, so check the numbers on the listing. Unlisted specs should be treated as unknown. Compare thickness and hardness before price when the label alone is the only claim you can see.

faq.q: Which heavy-duty shears are best overall?
faq.a: The MAD SHARK is the best for bones thanks to 3.5mm blades and a spring. The HOSHANHO is the best for edge life and handle feel. The SHAN ZU is the best for cleaning. Choose by your toughest job. If you are torn, choose by your toughest recurring task and add a lighter pair for everything else.

faq.q: Can heavy-duty shears cut chicken bones?
faq.a: Thick-blade poultry shears can cut small bones and joints. The MAD SHARK is the clearest fit. Harder steels like 57 HRC can chip if twisted against bone. Cut straight along the line of the bone. Wear no gloves with loose cuffs near a spring pair, and keep fingers clear of the blade path while cutting.

faq.q: Are wooden handles a good idea?
faq.a: A Pakkawood handle like the HOSHANHO feels premium and balanced. It should be hand washed rather than run in the dishwasher. Plastic handles such as the Gidli tolerate the machine. Choose by how you wash. A sheath or a drawer slot keeps wooden handles away from damp, which extends their life.

faq.q: Do I need a set or a single pair?
faq.a: A set such as the Gidli or DRAGON RIOT adds a seafood scissor, and the Astercook gives three pairs. A single shear like the MAD SHARK puts all the strength in one tool. Choose by household needs. Think about who else will use the tool, since a household with several cooks may benefit from the Astercook pack.

faq.q: How do I clean heavy-duty shears?
faq.a: Use hot soapy water or the dishwasher if the listing allows it. The SHAN ZU separates for deep cleaning. Follow USDA guidance for tools that touch raw poultry. Dry fully to prevent rust. A small brush reaches the pivot and the serrated edge more effectively than a sponge.

Eventually. Softer steels like 3Cr13 on the Gidli are easy to resharpen, while 57 HRC steels hold an edge longer. Serrated edges are harder to sharpen at home. Gentle washing helps. Keep a wet stone or a sharpening aid handy if you buy a softer steel, since touch-ups are quick.
